title: 2026 year-end tax: the family income threshold rises, but overseas proof still matters
summary: For 2026 income tax, Japan raises the income test for a dependent relative, same-household spouse and a single parent's qualifying child to ¥620,000 of total income—equivalent to ¥1.36 million when the person's income is salary only under the stated assumptions. For relatives living overseas, however, relationship and remittance evidence still determines whether a deduction can actually be claimed.
why_it_matters: Families can easily mix up three different things: the income-tax dependent threshold, social-insurance dependency and immigration/work limits. The tax threshold changes for 2026, but it does not automatically rewrite those other systems, and overseas-family deductions can fail if the required proof is missing.

claims.text: For 2026 and 2027 income tax, the income requirement for dependent relatives, same-household spouses and a single parent's qualifying child is ¥620,000 or less of total income; when income is salary only under the NTA table assumptions, the corresponding salary-revenue figure is ¥1.36 million or less.
The 2026 reform is generally effective from December 1, 2026 and is reflected in the December 2026 year-end adjustment; ordinary withholding through November is not changed by this reform.
To claim deductions for an overseas relative, the taxpayer may need relationship documents and remittance documents; foreign-language documents require Japanese translations under the NTA rules.

For an overseas relative aged 30 to under 70, ordinary dependent deduction generally requires that the person fit an allowed category such as qualifying study abroad, disability, or receiving at least ¥380,000 during the year for living or education expenses, with the specified supporting documents.

The safest practical interpretation is to treat ¥1.36 million as an income-tax figure only; a household should separately check social-insurance dependency, employment rules and immigration/work-permission limits rather than treating one threshold as universal.
claims.basis: The cited NTA material governs income tax, not the separate social-insurance or immigration systems

editorial_visual.scene: a Japanese year-end tax form on a kitchen table connected by a clean paper trail to remittance receipts and a family photo overseas, while separate labeled lanes imply tax, insurance and immigration are different systems without readable text
editorial_visual.caption: One income number does not control every family rule

content.key_message: For 2026 income tax, the salary-only dependent threshold can be ¥1.36 million, but do not confuse that with social-insurance or immigration limits—and keep overseas-family proof organized before year-end adjustment.
content.who_is_affected: Employees in Japan preparing 2026 year-end adjustment who claim a spouse/dependent, especially people supporting relatives who live in the Philippines or another country.
content.when: The reform is generally effective December 1, 2026 and affects the 2026 year-end adjustment. Overseas relationship/remittance documents should be collected during the year rather than reconstructed at the last minute.
content.financial_impact: The reform can change whether a relative fits the income-tax dependent test and therefore whether a deduction is available. The exact tax saving depends on the taxpayer, deduction category and taxable income; ALAM does not invent a universal yen saving.
content.risk_if_ignored: A taxpayer may omit a valid deduction, claim an invalid one, or discover too late that overseas relationship/remittance evidence is missing. A second risk is planning work hours around ¥1.36 million while accidentally breaching a separate insurance or immigration rule.
content.deadline: Prepare before your employer's 2026 year-end-adjustment document deadline; the NTA reform itself is reflected from December 2026. Employer submission dates vary, so use the date your payroll/HR office gives you.
content.effort: Medium: classify the relative, estimate 2026 income correctly, gather relationship/remittance evidence and submit the correct year-end forms.
content.potential_benefit: Correctly claiming a deduction you are entitled to while avoiding a later correction, payroll rejection or tax-office query.
content.downside: The ¥1.36 million salary-only figure is not a universal family-income wall. Applying it blindly to health insurance, pension or immigration can produce costly mistakes.
content.what_would_change_mind: A later NTA amendment to the 2026 reform, year-end forms or overseas-dependent documentation rules.

30 sec.what_happened: Japan raises the 2026 income-tax test for several family-dependent categories to ¥620,000 total income, equivalent to ¥1.36 million salary-only under the NTA table.
30 sec.why_it_matters: More families may fit the income-tax test, but overseas deductions still need proof and other systems use different rules.
30 sec.what_to_do_watch: Estimate the relative's 2026 income, save relationship/remittance documents and check tax, social insurance and immigration separately.
30 sec.bottom_line: ¥1.36 million is a tax number—not a universal permission to work or remain a dependent everywhere.

reading_levels.2_min: Japan's 2026 income-tax reform raises the family income test from ¥580,000 to ¥620,000 of total income; for salary-only income under the NTA table, that corresponds to ¥1.36 million instead of ¥1.23 million. The reform is generally implemented from December and reflected in 2026 year-end adjustment. For family living overseas, the deduction is not based on income alone: relationship and remittance documents are required, and relatives aged 30 to under 70 face additional category/document rules, including the ¥380,000 annual remittance route in applicable cases. This is income-tax law. Social-insurance dependency and immigration/work authorization must be checked separately.

outcomes: Distinguish total income from salary revenue in the NTA threshold table.
Explain why overseas-dependent proof and other systems must be checked separately.
learning.background: Japan's year-end adjustment lets many employees settle annual income tax through payroll. A dependent deduction is governed by tax-law definitions, not simply by whether a person is called a dependent in everyday life or on health insurance.

terms.meaning: A tax-law income measure after applying the relevant income calculation rules; it is not always the same as gross salary received.
terms.why_it_matters: The legal dependent test is stated as ¥620,000 total income, while ¥1.36 million is the salary-only revenue equivalent in the NTA table.

terms.meaning: Evidence showing money was sent for the overseas relative's living or education expenses as required by the NTA rules.
terms.why_it_matters: Without the required evidence, an otherwise-related overseas family member may not support the claimed deduction.

how_it_works.title: First classify the tax relationship
how_it_works.explanation: Spouse, dependent relative and special-relative categories have different income ranges and deduction calculations. Start with the correct tax category rather than one household label.

how_it_works.title: Then test income using tax definitions
how_it_works.explanation: For the core dependent-relative/same-household-spouse test, 2026 uses ¥620,000 total income. The ¥1.36 million number is specifically the salary-only revenue equivalent shown by the NTA.

how_it_works.title: Overseas claims add an evidence layer
how_it_works.explanation: You must establish the family relationship and required financial support. Some 30-to-under-70 overseas relatives need additional qualifying evidence such as study-abroad status, disability status or at least ¥380,000 of qualifying annual remittance.

learning.example: A mother in the Philippines with salary-only income of ¥1.24 million equivalent may fall within the new 2026 salary-only tax threshold where she did not under the prior ¥1.23 million figure, but the Japanese taxpayer still has to satisfy the overseas-relative rules and provide the required documents.
takeaways: 2026 core family tax threshold: ¥620,000 total income.
Salary-only equivalent in the NTA table: ¥1.36 million.
Overseas relatives still require relationship/remittance evidence.
Some overseas relatives age 30–69 have extra qualification/document rules.
Tax, social insurance and immigration are separate systems.

action_plan.goal: Submit a correct 2026 year-end family deduction claim with the evidence needed for any overseas relative.
action_plan.who_should_act: Employees who plan to claim a spouse/dependent or who support relatives overseas. If you do not claim family-related deductions, this checklist can be ignored.
action_plan.deadline: Use your employer's year-end-adjustment deadline; do not assume every company uses the same date.
prepare: Estimate of the relative's full-year 2026 income using the correct tax category.
Required relationship documents for an overseas relative and Japanese translations when required.
Remittance records showing support sent to each relevant overseas relative.
Any additional study-abroad/disability/¥380,000 remittance evidence required for an overseas relative age 30 to under 70.

steps.action: Identify the correct NTA category and whether the person lives in Japan or overseas.
steps.how: Use the NTA year-end materials rather than assuming health-insurance 'dependent' status determines income-tax treatment.
steps.done_when: You know which NTA category/rules apply.

steps.action: Estimate the relative's full-year income and compare it with the correct tax-law threshold.
steps.how: For salary-only income, use the NTA's salary-revenue equivalents; do not mix gross salary with total-income figures.
steps.done_when: The income test is documented using one consistent definition.

steps.action: Collect relationship, remittance and any extra category documents before payroll asks for them.
steps.how: Follow the NTA overseas-relative list; translate foreign-language relationship/supporting documents when required.
steps.done_when: You can show the required proof for each overseas relative you intend to claim.

mistakes_to_avoid: Calling ¥1.36 million a universal social-insurance or immigration wall.
Comparing gross salary directly with a threshold stated as total income without using the NTA conversion/rules.
Sending money but discarding the remittance evidence.
Assuming one lump remittance automatically proves support for multiple relatives.
Waiting until payroll deadline to discover foreign documents require translation or additional proof.

decision_rules.if: The relative is overseas and you cannot establish the required relationship/remittance evidence
decision_rules.then: Do not assume the deduction is valid; resolve the documentation issue before claiming it.

decision_rules.if: You are using the ¥1.36 million figure to decide work hours or dependent status
decision_rules.then: Check social-insurance and immigration/work rules separately before acting.

action_plan.follow_up: Keep copies of the forms and evidence after year-end adjustment in case payroll or the tax office asks for clarification, and update the claim if the relative's final 2026 income differs materially from the estimate.
